data.name: Shooty Squad
data.detailed_description:
Shooty Squad is a fast paced, competitive first person shooter with hilarious graphics and ragdoll physics.

With a variety of guns from machine guns, snipers or even RPG's. Beating your opponent will take not only quick reflexes, but being smart about how you play !

Learning the location and advantages of each gun, will be the key to winning against your opponents.

Each map has been designed with keeping the game as balanced as possible. Each map will have its own unique flow and personality !

reviews.review:
Shooty Squad is a compact multiplayer first-person shooter that favors quick action, straightforward mechanics, and humorous presentation over realism or complicated progression systems. Developed and published by Liam Doherty, the game approaches the arena shooter formula with an intentionally uncomplicated design. Players enter relatively small battlegrounds, search for useful weapons, learn the layout of each environment, and attempt to outgun their opponents. Its simplicity makes the basic experience easy to understand, while weapon placement and map knowledge provide some additional depth for players willing to learn its systems.

Combat revolves around a modest selection of firearms and explosive weapons scattered throughout the arenas. Instead of overwhelming players with a massive arsenal, the game keeps its weapon selection manageable, allowing each option to serve a recognizable purpose. Automatic weapons are useful during direct confrontations, longer-range firearms reward accuracy and positioning, and explosive equipment can quickly change the outcome of an encounter. Since weapons must be collected around the map, knowing where valuable equipment appears becomes an important advantage.

Movement and positioning are equally significant. Experienced players can memorize useful routes, weapon locations, and areas where opponents are likely to appear. This creates a traditional arena-shooter rhythm in which success comes from more than simply aiming quickly. Controlling useful sections of a map and anticipating enemy movement can be just as valuable as mechanical accuracy. The maps themselves are relatively straightforward, which makes them accessible but also means that the overall tactical variety eventually becomes limited.

The multiplayer component offers familiar modes including free-for-all, team deathmatch, and capture the flag. Free-for-all provides the most immediate experience, placing everyone against everyone else and rewarding aggressive play. Team deathmatch introduces cooperation without making the rules complicated, while capture the flag gives players an objective beyond collecting kills. The three modes are conventional, but they fit the game's uncomplicated approach and provide enough variation to change how players move around the arenas.

One of the more entertaining aspects of Shooty Squad is its humorous physics. Characters react to attacks with exaggerated ragdoll behavior, giving firefights a deliberately silly quality. The visual design is similarly modest and functional rather than technically impressive. This works reasonably well because the game never presents itself as a realistic military experience. Its personality instead comes from the contrast between recognizable shooter mechanics and the absurd results that can occur when characters are blasted around the environment.

An offline Zombie mode provides an alternative to competitive multiplayer. Fighting AI-controlled enemies changes the pace considerably because survival becomes more important than predicting the behavior of another human player. This mode is especially valuable considering the age and niche nature of the game, since finding an active public multiplayer population may not always be practical. It does not turn Shooty Squad into a substantial single-player shooter, but it gives players something meaningful to do without depending entirely on matchmaking.

The biggest weakness is its unfinished Early Access condition. The game originally entered Early Access with ambitions to receive additional maps, weapons, modes, balancing improvements, bug fixes, and other community-driven refinements. Development activity, however, has remained dormant for many years. As a result, it is better to evaluate Shooty Squad according to its existing content rather than what its Early Access roadmap once suggested it might eventually become. The limited amount of content becomes increasingly apparent during extended play, especially when the same maps, weapons, and modes begin repeating.

Its free-to-play availability makes those shortcomings considerably easier to accept. There is little financial risk involved in trying it, and players who enjoy older independent arena shooters may find some entertainment in its direct approach. Steam achievements provide additional objectives for completion-focused players, although achievements cannot compensate for the relatively narrow selection of activities. Shooty Squad works best in short sessions rather than as a multiplayer game intended to occupy hundreds of hours.

Steam Deck compatibility is Playable rather than fully Verified. The game can be used on Steam Deck, but the handheld experience may require adjustments such as community controller configurations, touchscreen interaction, or use of the virtual keyboard in certain situations. Some interface text may also be relatively small on the Deck's display. Players willing to make minor accommodations should still be able to experience the game, but it does not offer the completely seamless handheld integration associated with a Steam Deck Verified release.

Shooty Squad ultimately feels like a promising small multiplayer experiment that never expanded far beyond its original foundation. Its accessible shooting, weapon pickups, map-based strategy, humorous ragdolls, familiar competitive modes, and offline zombie activity give it enough personality to remain enjoyable in short bursts. The problem is longevity. Limited content and years of inactivity leave the experience feeling permanently unfinished, and its multiplayer emphasis makes the availability of other players an additional concern. Even so, there is charm in its uncomplicated design, particularly for anyone looking for a free arena shooter that can be learned almost immediately.

It is an entertaining but limited shooter with enjoyable fundamentals and amusing physics, held back primarily by its small scope and long-dormant Early Access development.

Rating: 7/10
